Primary concerns: latency SLOs for fraud-detection routes, data residency and KMS integration, and clear unit economics for bursty traffic. Agreed next steps: send pricing and benchmark artifacts, share security/compliance docs, and schedule a two-week pilot to run end-to-end tests.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-12 16:00 PT | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Ortiz (Solstice Head of ML), Liam Park (Solstice Platform Eng), Priya Shah (Solstice Security), Noah Green (PM)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate it. Um quick intros - I'm Alex, I'm the AE for this account, Samira is our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Samira Patel: Hi all, hi Maya, Liam, Priya, Noah, excited to walk through the Console today, show the per-route analytics and the cost breakdowns.
[00:15] Maya Ortiz: Thanks Alex, yeah we mainly wanna see how we can get visibility into the fraud-detection route, and understand tail latency and cost impact. We have pretty spiky traffic.
[00:25] Alex Chen: Totally, that's exactly what we built the per-route dashboards for. Quick agenda, we'll do a live Console walkthrough, look at route-level token usage, latency percentiles, cost allocation, then discuss batching/kv cache implications and security controls.
[00:40] Samira Patel: Jumping in — this is the Console home. Ignore the autopopulated demo data — but the left nav, you'll see Analytics -> Routes. I'll click into the fraud-detection route.
[00:50] [00:50] Samira Patel: Here's the route overview: request rate over time, tokens per request, and a cost attribution chart. Notice you can group by model variant, region, or deployment type (hosted vs dedicated).
[01:05] Liam Park: Quick Q - how precise is the cost attribution? Our finance team wants per-route $/day.
[01:10] Samira Patel: Good question. We compute cost by combining per-token runtime metrics, model compute profile (gflops/sec profile) and infra unit costs; we then allocate burst/overhead pro-rata. It's not perfect to the cent but it's usually within a few percent for planning.
[01:25] Maya Ortiz: Do you factor in batching gains? Because our average seq len is only 80 but batching could change per-token cost significantly.
[01:32] Samira Patel: Yes — Console shows two projections: observed cost and optimized projection if you enable batching + prefix cache. The projection assumes X% batching based on request concurrency. We also have a toggle for quantized model variants which changes the per-token cost.
[01:45] [01:45] Samira Patel: Here's the per-route breakdown table — latency p50/p95/p99, tokens in/out, cost per 1k requests and cumulative spend for the selected window.
[02:00] Priya Shah: On security, does the Console display any PII? We need to ensure audit logs are available and KMS integration for customer keys.
[02:08] Alex Chen: We log token counts and route identifiers but do not persist full user inputs by default. For Private deployments we offer customer-managed KMS and audit-log forwarding to your SIEM. We'll share the SOC 2 and KMS docs after the call.
[02:22] Noah Green: Also curious about role-based access in the Console — can we lock down who sees cost vs who sees raw transcripts?
[02:30] Samira Patel: Yes, RBAC is configurable. You can give finance read-only cost views, while limiting transcript access to security/ops. SSO/SAML works with SCIM provisioning.
[02:42] [02:42] Maya Ortiz: Could you show an example of a migrating route from hosted to dedicated — how do cost/latency numbers change?
[02:50] Samira Patel: Sure — switching this example route to Dedicated reduces p95 from ~420ms to ~210ms in this synthetic trace, and cost per token shifts depending on reserved capacity utilization. If you have steady throughput, Dedicated gives predictable unit cost; for spiky workloads hosted with autoscale might be cheaper at baseline but more variable.
[03:10] Liam Park: Are those numbers based on your internal benchmarks or customer data?
[03:14] Samira Patel: It's a mix; Console can import your benchmark run or we can run a pilot to capture your real traffic. We recommend a short pilot so the model selection and kernel/quantization recommendations are tailored.
[03:26] [03:26] Alex Chen: On the point of model variants — we often provide a family of compatible model sizes. The Console's Optimize tab will recommend whether a quantized 4-bit variant hits your quality bar with much lower cost.
[03:40] Maya Ortiz: For fraud-detection, the precision loss is scary. How do you validate quality regressions?
[03:46] Samira Patel: We tie quality monitoring to your prompt sets and evals. Console can run regression alerts if a model or quantization change increases false positives above your threshold. You can pin routes to a model version and perform canary rollouts with automatic fallback.
[04:02] [04:02] Priya Shah: For compliance, we need data residency in EU for some routes. Can we route EU traffic to EU-only dedicated pools?
[04:10] Samira Patel: Yes, routing policies can be region-bound. You can create route-level policies that enforce region and tier, and have automated fallback to a different tier if capacity is exhausted.
[04:22] Maya Ortiz: Show me the cost breakdown export — we want CSVs for our chargeback system.
[04:28] Samira Patel: Click Export CSV — you get per-route per-model entries with tokens, compute seconds, and cost columns. We also include an attribution note about shared overhead.
[04:40] [04:40] Noah Green: Any way to see token-level heatmaps to identify hot prompts?
[04:44] Samira Patel: We have a prompt analytics panel — it shows frequent prefixes and average tokens consumed. It's helpful for tuning prompts and caching.
[04:55] Maya Ortiz: Does Redwood handle KV cache for long conversations or do we manage it?
[05:00] Samira Patel: The runtime handles KV caching for autoregressive decoders; prefix caching is configurable. Sometimes the transcript misstates it as 'KV cash' — it's KV cache.
[05:10] [05:10] Alex Chen: Let's talk pilot and benchmarks — Maya, what do you consider success for the pilot?
[05:14] Maya Ortiz: Two things: must meet p95 < 250ms on fraud route and cost per 1k requests should be within 20% of our target modeled budget. Also zero incidents on data leakage concerns.
[05:26] Alex Chen: Good, we'll design the pilot around that. Samira will run a recommended config and null test.
[05:34] Samira Patel: For the pilot we'll need representative traffic, sample prompts, and acceptance criteria. We'll also run a small dedicated pool if you want to validate steady-state latency.
[05:45] [05:45] Liam Park: How intrusive is the Private deployment? We have air-gapped requirements for a subset of workloads.
[05:52] Samira Patel: Private has a customer-managed control plane option; deployment can be VPC or on-prem; we can integrate with your KMS/HSM. There's more setup time but it meets stricter compliance.
[06:05] Maya Ortiz: Any competitors that do this better? We've talked to Anthropic and a few managed infra vendors.
[06:11] Alex Chen: Market is busy — Anthropic/OpenAI/Vertex have offerings; our differentiation is the unified Console, model lifecycle tooling and cost-aware controls.
[06:20] [06:20] Priya Shah: On encryption — at rest, in transit, and customer key control?
[06:25] Samira Patel: Encrypted at rest and in transit by default; for hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS. For dedicated/private you can bring your own key.
[06:36] Alex Chen: I'll drop the SOC 2 and KMS docs in the secure link.
[06:40] [06:40] Samira Patel: Back to Console — here's the Optimize recommendations. It suggests enabling batching windows for this route to improve throughput, and recommends a 4-bit quantized flavor for non-sensitive helper routes.
[06:55] Maya Ortiz: So we can mix model variants per route? For example, use full precision for fraud and quantized for other less sensitive flows?
[07:02] Samira Patel: Exactly. Route-level model pinning lets you pick different variants. And you can set automated fallbacks — if a variant fails quality checks, we roll back to the previous version.
[07:15] [07:15] Noah Green: Can the Console surface cost anomalies — e.g., sudden spike because of a runaway prompt?
[07:19] Samira Patel: Yes, we have anomaly detection on token spend with alerting integration (PagerDuty/Slack). You can set thresholds per route.
[07:28] Maya Ortiz: Could we get a quick demo of the alerts config?
[07:31] Samira Patel: Sure — Alerts -> Create -> choose metric (tokens / cost / p95) -> set window and threshold -> choose notification channel.
[07:40] [07:40] Alex Chen: Alright, let's recap before Qs.
[07:43] Alex Chen: Next steps — I'll send tailored pricing and per-route cost CSV; Samira will share benchmark template and runbook; Priya we'll share SOC 2/KMS docs; we'll target a pilot start week of 2026-04-27.
[07:58] Priya Shah: We'll confirm security contacts and provide a shortlist of required compliance docs.
[08:03] Maya Ortiz: We'll prepare sample traffic and the prompt set — thanks.
[08:08] Liam Park: One last question — do you have a changelog for runtime kernel choices? We need transparency on compilation/quantization kernels used.
[08:14] Samira Patel: Yes, Optimize includes a model profile and kernel selection notes — we'll include that with the benchmark artifacts.
[08:22] [08:22] Alex Chen: Great. Any other blockers?
[08:25] Noah Green: none from me.
[08:27] Maya Ortiz: No. Thanks, this was helpful.
[08:30] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and pricing.
[08:34] [08:34] Call ended

Notes: transcript contains occasional mishearings (KV cash, autopopulated) and generic speaker attribution at times. References: shared deck (link: redwood.com/deck/console-demo), benchmark template (link: redwood.com/benchmarks/template.xlsx), SOC2/KMS doc (to be sent via secure share).
